title: Write the rule
hookLine: one page, kept where you'll see it
tomorrow: what was the very first prayer this path taught you?

lines: WRITE THE VISION, MAKE IT PLAIN.
cards: A sticky note on a mirror. Three words on a lock screen. A coach's game plan on one laminated card.

Some things are written so you can't miss them. The prophet Habakkuk is told to do exactly that, in the Douay-Rheims: "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables: that he that readeth it may run over it." Run?
Why would a prophet write so a runner could read it?

teach.h: WRITE THE VISION, MAKE IT PLAIN.
teach.b: Some readers take it this way: write it so large and plain that someone running past can take it in at a glance.

teach.h: SO A RUNNER CAN READ IT.
teach.b: Others read it as: so the one who reads it can run, carrying the message on. Either way, the vision isn't buried in a long scroll. It's short, plain and out where people pass.

teach.h: ON THE DOORS OF THY HOUSE.
teach.b: Moses says the same about God's words: "thou shalt write them in the entry, and on the doors of thy house."

One to tell a friend: Jewish tradition keeps that verse with a mezuzah, a small case on the doorpost holding those very words. Benedict asked that his Rule be read aloud often, so no one could say he didn't know it.
A rule you can't remember can't guide you. That's where this stretch lands.

Fifteen days built a rule: what already works, a time and place to pray, Sunday at the center, a rhythm for confession, scripture daily, regular mercy, a book, your people, a guide, a little hunger, a portion, holy leisure, company for the road, and a rule that bends.
Now it goes on one page. One short line each, plain enough to read on the run.

how: Catholics who keep a personal rule of life often write it on a single page or card, review it with a confessor or spiritual director, and revisit it at the start of Advent or Lent.

games.q: your rule fits on one page. a friend says frame it in the living room; you'd rather tape it inside your closet door. what matters most?
o: that other people can see it and hold you to it.
that it's framed nicely, so it feels official.
that it's somewhere you'll actually pass every day.
games.why: Moses said write them in the entry, on the doors: where you pass. who else sees it matters less than whether you do.

practice: Take one sheet of paper and write your rule, one short line per piece: when you pray, Sunday, confession, a reading, service, a book, your people, a guide, a fast, a portion, rest, a saint. If a line runs long, shrink it.
Then fold the page once and decide where it will live.

wordCard.voice: Write the rule. Fifteen days of pieces on one plain page, kept where you'll pass it every day.

orig.note: Latin: a rule. the word in the title of Benedict's Regula, his Rule for monks.

carryVoice: Keep this: one page, plain enough to read on the run, and yours now. See you tomorrow.
